clue.text: Potential national anthem encapsulating the folly in conflict

definitions.text: Potential national anthem encapsulating the folly in conflict

indicators.note: potential describes something not yet formed, so these letters are only the raw stuff of a new word
letters in conflict are thrown into disorder, signalling that the pooled words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A proposed new anthem that captures the madness of war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potential' and 'in conflict' both signal the shuffle of N, ANTHEM, THE and FOLLY. Read whole, the clue also describes the answer: a song for war dead, born of wartime folly.
explanation.definitionFit: A song honouring soldiers killed in war might well be adopted as a country's anthem, and it springs from the folly of conflict.

clue.text: Hotel gym's opening: the girl we brought up has to work out to maintain it?

definitions.text: Hotel gym's opening: the girl we brought up has to work out to maintain it?

parts.note: H is Hotel in the radio alphabet

indicators.note: has means holds, so the daughter phrase contains the gym's first letter

parts.note: a daughter raised by the speakers is 'our lass', northern English for our girl

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: to figure something out is to work it out

explanation.surface: At the hotel gym's launch, a proud family's daughter must exercise to keep her shape.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue explains why the girl works out: to keep a curvy shape, narrow at the waist.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's shape with full bust and hips and a narrow waist, like a sand timer, is often kept up by exercise.

clue.text: Add up boxes circulating top-notch features

indicators.note: boxes means encloses, so the turned word goes round the shuffled letters
in a down clue up means the word is read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: to add is to sum

indicators.note: circulating means going round and round, so the letters of top-notch are moved about

explanation.surface: An accountant tots up boxes while first-rate features go round.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' reads the word for add from bottom to top; 'circulating' jumbles top-notch, and 'boxes' wraps the first around the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Mutton chops are bushy side whiskers, a facial feature broadening towards the jaw.

clue.text: "Frisky nature" describes a spring newborn

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so the shuffled letters go around a
frisky means lively and playful, prompting the letters to jump about

explanation.surface: A playful temperament is said to characterise a baby born in spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frisky' rearranges NATURE into TAUREN, and 'describes' puts it round A. Taurus runs from late April to late May.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone born under the zodiac sign of the Bull, in late spring, is described by this astrological term.

clue.text: Certainly on one's own this time

parts.note: in rhyming slang Tod Sloan stands for own, so on one's tod means on one's own
ay is an old or dialect word for yes, certainly

explanation.surface: Someone insists they will certainly be alone this time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On your tod' is everyday British slang for on your own; the phrase's last word supplies the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The word refers to the present day or present era, the current occasion.

clue.text: Listened in fearful awe, prepared to bury head

indicators.note: the head letter of the second piece is buried deeper inside the combined letters

parts.note: fearful marks a jumbling of awe, its three letters shaken into a new order
a rigged scheme has been prepared or fixed in advance

explanation.surface: Someone eavesdropped, frightened, ready to hide their face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fearful' turns AWE into EAW; with RIGGED that is EAWRIGGED, and 'bury head' moves R, the head of RIGGED, back one place.
explanation.definitionFit: To earwig is British slang for eavesdropping, overhearing others' conversation on the quiet.

clue.text: Roman general who's keeping people enthralled in the auditorium?

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience hears, so the phrase is judged by its sound

parts.note: one keeping an audience enthralled is a gripper, something that grips

explanation.surface: A Roman general holds his audience spellbound in the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic accent 'a gripper' and the general's name sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa was the military commander who won Actium for Octavian, later Augustus.

clue.text: Press put out fake news?

parts.note: what newspapers print that is knowingly false is an untruth

explanation.surface: Did the newspapers publish false stories?
explanation.definitionFit: Fake news printed by the press is a falsehood, a deliberate untruth.

clue.text: Yet more playing on it, one sharing out cuts

definitions.text: Yet more playing on it, one sharing out cuts

indicators.note: cuts means slices into, so the shuffled pair and the sharer go inside the word for yet more

parts.note: nay is used to mean 'or rather, yet more', as in 'many, nay hundreds'

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters of on it are toyed with

parts.note: an allotter is one who allots, sharing out portions

explanation.surface: Ever more people play the lottery, while the organisers share out the proceeds in cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' jumbles ON IT and 'cuts' sends both pieces into the word for yet more. Read whole, the clue describes the draw: more and more play it, and one body shares out the takings.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's state-run draw has millions of players, and its operator distributes shares of the takings to winners and good causes.

clue.text: Awful toys unwrapped in December

indicators.note: unwrapped strips the outer layers from the phrase Awful toys, leaving the letters at its core

explanation.surface: Christmas presents turn out dreadful when opened in December.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip three letters from each end of AWFULTOYS. The abbreviation ult. (ultimo) means 'of last month', so in a letter dated in January, as this puzzle was, it refers to December.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultimo, abbreviated ult., marks a date in the previous month, which for January correspondence is December.

clue.text: Bloody Duke, repelled in rebellion, apprehended

indicators.note: in places the turned-round pieces inside the word for rebellion

parts.note: unrest is popular rebellion or agitation

indicators.note: repelled means driven back, so the steak word and the duke are read backwards

parts.note: a bloody steak is rare

explanation.surface: A brutal duke, driven back during an uprising, is captured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repelled' turns the steak word and D round together, giving DERAR, and 'in' sets that inside the word for rebellion.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone apprehended by police has been taken into custody, the state of being detained.

clue.text: Grand centrepiece missing from garden shop

indicators.note: the middle letter of the garden word is removed, its centrepiece gone

parts.note: a rockery is a garden of stones and alpine plants

explanation.surface: A garden shop whose grand central display has disappeared.
explanation.walkthrough: The garden word has seven letters, so its centrepiece is the fourth, K; 'centrepiece missing from' removes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A grocery is a store selling food and household goods, a kind of retail outlet.

clue.text: Nimrod's too old for love and laying it on thick

parts.note: the setter Nimrod refers to himself, so Nimrod's (Nimrod is) gives I'M
someone past it is too old for something
love is nil in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: The setter admits he is too old for romance yet keeps overdoing the flattery.
explanation.walkthrough: Nimrod is the setter's pseudonym, so 'Nimrod's' is the setter saying I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Impasto is the painting technique of applying pigment in heavy layers, literally spreading it thickly.

clue.text: Having flipped, turtle did as cricket did?

indicators.note: a flipped turtle is turned over, so the letters are turned about

explanation.surface: A turtle, on its back, copies a cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having flipped' rearranges TURTLE DID AS. The question mark marks a definition by example: the insect is one of many that make this noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Crickets chirp by rubbing their wings or legs together, making a shrill grating sound.

clue.text: Blood carrier somehow contains drainage, one in drops

indicators.note: somehow says the letters arrive by some unstated rearrangement
drops says one of the two-letter groups spelling in is let fall from the pool before shuffling

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A blood vessel apparently holds drainage, and one drop falls in.
explanation.walkthrough: CONTAINS and DRAINAGE each hold IN; 'one in drops' removes one of them, and the remaining fourteen letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the first section of the body's main artery, rising from the heart and carrying oxygenated blood.

clue.text: Wimbledon's finalist — not No.1 — lived frustrated with lawn game

definitions.text: Wimbledon's finalist — not No.1 — lived frustrated with lawn game

indicators.note: frustrated means thwarted and upset, so the letters are thrown into disorder
the finalist of a word is its last letter
the No.1 letter of Wimbledon is W, and that letter is not wanted in the lawn

explanation.surface: A Wimbledon finalist who never won lived thwarted by the grass-court game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not No.1' drops W from LAWN; 'frustrated' rearranges LIVED + LAN. The 1980s world number one reached two Wimbledon finals but never took the title, preferring clay to grass.
explanation.definitionFit: The Czech-born champion won eight majors yet lost both his Wimbledon finals, so his grass-court career ended in frustration.

clue.text: See 14
In moments that pass too briefly, news of Spartacus?

indicators.note: In places the news word inside the grains of time

parts.note: the sands of time are the passing moments, as in an hourglass
word means news, as in 'any word from her?'

indicators.note: briefly cuts the last letter off the phrase for too

parts.note: and all is a colloquial phrase meaning too, as well

explanation.surface: News of the gladiator Spartacus arrives in moments that slip by all too fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' clips AND ALL to ANDAL. Spartacus (1960) is the classic example of the film genre, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Sword-and-sandal is the label for epic films set in ancient Rome or Greece, and Spartacus is a famous instance.

clue.text: In service, floater and stinger leading a double life

indicators.note: In sets the boxer inside the word for service

parts.note: duty is service owed, as in military duty
Muhammad Ali promised to float like a butterfly and sting like a bee

explanation.surface: Serving in some capacity, a floater and a stinger lead a secret double existence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'floater and stinger' points to Ali's boast 'float like a butterfly, sting like a bee'.
explanation.definitionFit: Duality is the state of being twofold, of having two natures or sides.

clue.text: See 17
Self-esteem given a boost being received by a god of the highest order

indicators.note: being received by means taken in, so the turned word goes inside the god phrase

parts.note: Pan is the Greek god of the wild

indicators.note: in a down clue a boost lifts the word up, reading it backwards

parts.note: ego is a person's sense of self-esteem

explanation.surface: A deity of the top rank welcomes a worshipper whose ego has been lifted.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'given a boost' lifts a word so it reads upwards; 'being received by' puts the result inside the god phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Apogean relates to the apogee, the point in an orbit farthest from Earth, figuratively the highest point.

clue.text: Diminutive Sergeant-Major coming to barracks

indicators.note: a barracks houses soldiers, so it holds the sergeant-major inside

parts.note: coming to a total is amounting to it in all

explanation.surface: A short sergeant-major arrives at the barracks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barracks' looks like a noun, but here it is a verb: it houses the soldier inside the phrase for coming to.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done in small is done on a reduced scale, in miniature.

clue.text: Recalled from Hotel to organise minor branch

indicators.note: Recalled says the hidden letters are read backwards
from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone is called back from a hotel to sort out a small branch office.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft left 'from' as a link word; it is the hidden-word indicator, so it is now named on the op.
explanation.definitionFit: A rootlet is a small subsidiary root, an offshoot of a plant's main root.

clue.text: Something you might find puzzling on public transport

parts.note: re means about, concerning, so on in the sense 'a talk on art'
a bus is a form of public transport

explanation.surface: A passenger finds something baffling on the bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puzzling' reads as bewildering, but it means used in puzzles.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture puzzle that represents words with images and letters, a staple of puzzle pages.

clue.text: Restricting sodium, scribbled a blue line which cannot be removed

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so the shuffled letters close around the sodium symbol
scribbled suggests a hasty, messy rewriting of the letters

parts.note: Na is the chemical symbol for sodium

explanation.surface: Cutting down on salt, someone scrawled a blue line that will not rub out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scribbled' turns A BLUE LINE into ULIENABLE, and 'Restricting' wraps it round NA.
explanation.definitionFit: An unalienable right is one that can never be taken away or transferred, a variant of inalienable.

clue.text: This port is warm and dry, did you say?

indicators.note: did you say asks how the phrase sounds when spoken

parts.note: to air washing is to warm and dry it thoroughly

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a port has a warm, dry climate.
explanation.walkthrough: Ayr is a port town on the west coast of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish town on the Firth of Clyde has a harbour, making it a seaport.

clue.text: Just five letters and a digit

indicators.note: just means only, leaving the five-letter span with nothing beyond it once the a is set aside

parts.note: a span of five letters from the start of the alphabet, written as a range from its first letter to its fifth

explanation.surface: A note that is merely five letters and a number.
explanation.walkthrough: Five letters are 'A to E'; with the clue's 'a' set aside, just 'to E' remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the five jointed members at the end of the foot is a digit, like a finger.

clue.text: Now trading has ceased prematurely, rebrand as Lily Grey and Co

indicators.note: to rebrand is to give a new identity, so the letters take a new form

explanation.surface: A shop ends trading early and relaunches under a new company name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rebrand' rearranges AS LILY GREY AND CO. Early-closing day was the weekday when British shops shut at lunchtime.
explanation.definitionFit: On that weekly half-day, shops in British towns stopped trading in the afternoon, before their usual hour.
